directives.directive: Channel Refik Anadol's data-flow aesthetic. Massively increase particle count (target 200k+ via GPGPU FBO if not already present). Replace any noise-driven motion with a smooth, slow flow field that feels LIKE pouring data — particles should look like a ML-trained machine dreaming. Palette: pearlescent cyan-violet duotone with white-hot core highlights. Add subtle bloom-feeling additive glow. No hard edges anywhere. The result should feel architectural in scale even without architecture in the scene.

Channel Casey Reas (Process compendium / Software Structures). Strip color saturation entirely — output must be near-monochrome (single dominant hue 0.0-0.15 saturation) with ONE small accent color used sparingly. Replace any noise with a deterministic rule-based emergence (cellular automaton, agent-based steering with simple local rules, or Reas's 'process 11' style — agents leaving traces). Embrace stillness and restraint. No sparkle, no glow excess. The form should feel like generative art from 2010, not 2025.

Channel Tyler Hobbs (Fidenza / Subscapes). Replace whatever motion exists with a structured, hand-tuned flow field — particles flow along clearly visible streamlines that DON'T overlap (use collision detection or domain partitioning so streams don't cross). Composition matters: leave significant negative space, group particles into 5-8 distinct color regions. Palette: warm earth tones (raw umber, terracotta, ochre, oxide red) with one cool accent. The piece should look like an OIL PAINTING that happens to be code, not a digital effect.

Channel Manolo Gamboa Naon's geometric aesthetic. Remove all noise functions, all curl-noise, all randomness from MOTION. Replace particle distribution with hard-edged geometric primitives: triangles, rings, half-circles, hexagons, lines — composed in a clear visual hierarchy. Color blocking: 3-5 flat colors, no gradients. Use the canvas like a 1970s editorial poster. If the piece had organic features, replace them with their geometric abstractions (e.g., a tree → stacked triangles).

Channel Memo Akten — physics-driven, atmospheric, slow temporal evolution, sublime. Replace any 'snappy' interaction response with smooth integration over multiple seconds (LERP toward target with low alpha). Particles should have momentum and inertia. Add a slow-rotating environment — feel like the camera is on a rail moving through a scene that has DEPTH (foreground particles, background fog). Palette: cool blues, deep teals, oceanic. The piece should feel like staring at the ocean at dusk, not a tech demo.

CROSS-POLLINATE: borrow the DOMINANT VISUAL SIGNATURE of a different favorited piece (from this list: 'n8q' Stanford Lucy figure, 'zs4' Lorenz attractor, '2n2' Aizawa attractor, 'w64' Lee Perry Smith head, 'kam' cypress↔art-deco morph, '8ug' audio-reactive shells, '7ea' differential growth, 'x09' L-system tree). Pick ONE that is most different from the current parent's direction. Now produce a child that COMBINES the parent's structural form with the chosen sibling's visual language (palette, motion law, or rendering technique — pick the most distinctive one). The result should feel like neither pure parent — something new emerges from the combination. The parent's RECOGNIZABLE FORM (statue, attractor shape, tree silhouette, etc.) should still be readable. State which sibling was chosen in a brief code comment at the top.

Add atmospheric depth: enable THREE.FogExp2 with density 0.025-0.040 matched to scene background color, and add a volumetric light beam by rendering a tall thin Cone mesh with a custom translucent additive shader (vertical, off-center top-left or top-right). Light intensity should be visible but not dominant — particles INTERSECTING the beam should brighten. This is a single, definite, cinematic light source — not generic ambient lighting.

Convert this piece from single-state (or A↔B morph) into a MULTI-CLICK CYCLE through {n} distinct visual states. Each click advances to the next state with a short cross-fade. States should be MEANINGFULLY different in form, not just palette swaps — different geometry, different motion law, or different particle distribution. Display the current state name in the bottom-right.

Channel Sage Jenson (mxsage) — physarum slime-mold simulation. Replace whatever motion the piece has with an agent-based system: each particle is an agent that (1) deposits a small amount of pheromone into a 2D trail texture, (2) senses pheromone density at three small offsets ahead-left, ahead, ahead-right, and (3) steers toward the strongest. Use a feedback texture (ping-pong RT) for the pheromone field with slight diffusion + decay each frame. Render the trail as the visual — organic webs, neural-net-like structure, biological feel. This is the SOTA fxhash aesthetic from 2024-2025.

Channel Jared Tarbell's 'Substrate' algorithm. Spawn lines from random edge points; each line grows perpendicular forward. When a line crosses an existing line, it stops AND spawns a new line at the crossing point at 90 degrees. Iterate until coverage. Render the resulting line graph as particle clusters along each segment with subtle color variation per generation. Result: architectural maze, urban-organic, recognizably algorithmic but warm.

Reject smoothness — embrace deliberate imperfection per the 2025-2026 'naïve painting' / 'anti-polish' counter-trend. Add hand-drawn-feeling irregularities: 8-12% per-particle position jitter, slight asymmetry where the piece was symmetric, off-grid placement, visible 'mark-making' (some particles much larger or denser than the field, like brushstrokes). The piece should look like a human's hand on top of code, not a polished AI-generated render.

Disrupted-grid composition (per 2026 design counter-trend against optimized layouts): if the piece has any regular pattern, symmetry, or smooth distribution, deliberately break it in 3-4 specific places — empty zones, density spikes, off-center accents, broken edges. The 'scuffs' should look intentional, not random — like pulled threads in a weave.

Update on a slow schedule (every 30s) — the piece becomes a living visualization.

Add an FxHash-style parameter panel: 4-6 sliders (top-right corner, minimal styling) that control distinct aspects of the piece in real time — particle count, motion intensity, palette hue rotation, fog density, motion law mix ratio, etc. Each slider has a visible label and current value. The piece becomes an instrument the viewer plays with, not just observes.

Channel dynamic-systems theory. Replace the motion law with a coupled-ODE system showing PHASE-SPACE STRUCTURE and BIFURCATION. Pick one: {system}. Bind pointer X to the control parameter so the user can drive the system through regimes (stable fixed point → limit cycle → period-doubling → chaos). Render the trajectory through phase space — the SHAPE of the orbit IS the visual. Transitions through bifurcations should be visible. Avoid hiding the system behind decoration; the math should be the form.
params: double-pendulum chaos (two coupled angular ODEs, sensitivity to initial conditions)
Lotka-Volterra predator-prey with 3 species (limit cycles, extinction events)
Kuramoto coupled oscillators on a graph (synchronization phase transition)

directives.directive: Channel Chiharu Shiota's thread-installation aesthetic. Render with LINES instead of points: replace THREE.Points with THREE.LineSegments (or many THREE.Line objects); each segment connects two anchor positions in space. Mass count: 8000-20000 segments. Each line is a single straight thread — no curves. Anchor strategy: pick {anchor}. Palette: Shiota's signature is dense red (crimson #9c1f1f), or pure white on black, or pure black on white — pick ONE color, stay near monochrome. Use LineBasicMaterial with low opacity (0.06-0.12) and additive blending so the network reads as gauzy volume. The whole field should feel like emotional infrastructure — threads as memory, connection, tension, distance. Suspend in architectural-feeling space (extra negative space at top, threads pooling at bottom). Subtle sway under pointer/audio is OK; the threads should remain readable as discrete strands.
params: every line connects a particle position to its nearest-neighbor in 3D — produces a dense weave around the form
every line connects a particle position to a fixed central anchor (or one of 3-5 anchors) — produces radiating bursts converging on architectural foci
every line connects two random particles in the field — produces a sparse Erdős-Rényi 'mind-map' web
lines connect each particle to its 3 nearest neighbors — creates a triangulated mesh feel, like tensile fabric
lines spawn from a recognizable object's surface (sampled via MeshSurfaceSampler) and reach toward a second anchor cluster — Shiota's signature 'object-tied' configuration

directives.directive: Replace point-sprite rendering with LINE-SEGMENT rendering. Wherever the parent piece uses THREE.Points + PointsMaterial / custom point shader, switch to THREE.LineSegments + LineBasicMaterial (or a custom line shader that supports per-segment color). Each segment connects either (a) consecutive particles along a path, (b) each particle to its nearest neighbor, or (c) each particle to a designated anchor — pick whichever fits the parent's existing form. KEEP the parent's motion law and palette logic. Tune line opacity to 0.08-0.18 and rely on additive blending so the network reads as accumulated linear weight, not noise. The piece should now feel woven instead of dotted.

Channel plane-based color-field art. Render the form as PLANES (translucent quads / sheets / volumetric layers), not points or lines. Use THREE.InstancedMesh of small PlaneGeometry instances, each oriented either billboarded-to-camera or aligned to a local normal field. Pick one artist as the aesthetic anchor: {artist}. Stay near monochrome or two-color (saturated, low value contrast). Use additive blending with low per-instance opacity (0.04-0.10) so OVERLAP IS THE COMPOSITION — the deeper the stack of overlapping planes, the brighter and more saturated the local color. The piece should feel like LIGHT, not particles — Turrell's 'we eat light, drink it through our skins.'
params: James Turrell — luminous color-field volumes you would stand inside (Aten Reign at the Guggenheim). Stratified horizontal bands of translucent color, smooth gradients between bands, soft cyan-magenta-amber transitions. The form should feel inhabitable.

Mark Rothko — large stacked horizontal rectangles, soft soaked edges, emotional weight from minimal vocabulary. 2-3 dominant color bands; bottom band weight, top band lightness; 'soaked-stain' edges via per-instance position jitter at band borders. Vermilion-on-maroon, plum-on-orange, slate-on-rust.

Olafur Eliasson — atmospheric volumetric planes. Sun-disc as a saturated single hue (sodium-amber for The Weather Project), surrounded by translucent fog-like sheets that catch implied directional light. Fog density should be visible as the plane-stack accumulates depth.

Yves Klein — monochrome saturated planes, IKB International Klein Blue (#002fa7). One color, many planes, no other element. The composition is COVERAGE, not COMPOSITION — uniform blue field broken only by subtle density variations and sparse breath-marks.

Carmen Herrera — hard-edge minimalism. Two flat colors, one geometric division line, that's it. Translate to particle space: planes split into two color regions divided by a clean diagonal/circular boundary; no gradients; no jitter. Restraint is the work.

Helen Frankenthaler — soak-stain. Thin diluted color washes that seep into raw canvas. Translate: planes with per-instance random rotation and position jitter, very low opacity, watercolor-feel; the boundary between color regions is feathered, not crisp.

directives.directive: Replace point-sprite rendering with PLANE/SHEET rendering. Each particle becomes a small InstancedMesh of PlaneGeometry (or BufferGeometry of two triangles). Orientation strategy: pick (a) billboarded to camera (always-facing, gives bokeh-disk feel), (b) aligned to a local field normal (gives flake/foliage feel — each plane catches light differently), or (c) all parallel to a reference plane (gives stratified-layers feel). Per-instance color from the parent's palette logic. Per-instance opacity 0.04-0.12 so OVERLAP IS COMPOSITION — dense regions read as brighter saturated pools, sparse regions read as gauze. KEEP the parent's motion law unchanged; only the rendering primitive changes. The piece should now feel like accumulating washes of light, not falling dust.

Channel Nicolas Bourriaud's RELATIONAL AESTHETICS (1998) — art whose substrate is human relation, social context, encounter. Translate to digital: the piece must respond to a SECOND viewer or external presence — open a WebSocket to a public broadcast (e.g. wss://stream.binance.com price ticker, public chat relay), or use BroadcastChannel API so multiple browser tabs of the piece on the same machine influence each other in real time. The visual reflects the SHARED state, not a private one. Display the count of active connections / external pulses in the corner. The work is the SOCIAL FIELD it creates, not the pixels.

Channel Timothy Morton's DARK ECOLOGY — art reckoning with hyperobjects (climate, mass extinction, deep time) at human scale. Translate: bind the piece to a slow real or simulated trajectory that exceeds human pacing — geological-time particle drift, exponential CO₂ growth curve as a deformation field, mass-extinction count as a particle-cull rate, pre-Cambrian → present timeline as a slow morph. The viewer should feel SCALE THEY CAN'T HOLD. Palette: muted earth tones bleeding into dead grey; never spectacle. A small running counter (years elapsed in piece-time, particles culled, etc.) reminds the viewer of what they cannot see directly.

Channel CCRU-era HYPERSTITION (Land, Plant, Fisher) — fictions that loop back into reality, machine-aesthetics dialed past human comfort. Translate: deliberately faster-than-pleasant motion, jungle/breakcore-tempo updates (~160 BPM rhythmic events), TR-808 click/snap visual hits on bass-band audio if mic granted, late-90s dark-rave palette (acid green, cyan, magenta on black), no soft falloff — hard edges, square-wave brightness, looping captions in monospace declaring future tense ('THE OUTSIDE WILL HAVE BEEN'). The piece overwhelms; it doesn't ask permission.

Channel Graham Harman's OBJECT-ORIENTED ONTOLOGY — objects WITHDRAW from full apprehension; no perspective fully captures the thing. Translate: the form should be partially visible, partially occluded — fog at variable density, depth that exceeds the camera's frustum, particles disappearing past a near-clip plane and reappearing rotated, a recognizable form (a statue, a tree) that the camera circles but never fully reveals. Add 3-4 'shy zones' where particles fade as the camera approaches. The viewer leaves with knowing it's something but not what.

Channel the SUBLIME (Burke/Kant tradition, re-engaged by Turrell, Kapoor, Eliasson) — overwhelming scale, awe mixed with terror, the small viewer in vast space. Translate: implied vastness via aggressive depth (camera near-clip very close, fog density very low so particles recede to infinity), single luminous point or thin band against dominant void, slow drift through what feels like infinite distance, no recognizable scale references. Sound (if mic enabled): low-frequency rumble visualization. The piece should make the viewer feel small.

Channel GLITCH AESTHETICS (Rosa Menkman, Beflix, datamoshing tradition) — embracing breakdown, error, compression artifact as THE aesthetic, not the failure of it. Translate: deliberately introduce JPEG-style 8x8 block artifacts in regions of the field, RGB channel separation (chromatic aberration that exceeds tasteful), occasional frame-skip / jitter / scrubbing-ahead bursts, zalgo-like vertical pixel-stretches on impact events, palette quantized to 4-6 colors with visible posterization. The work asserts that error is information.

Channel SLOW ART (Slow Art Day movement, Olafur Eliasson's pacing) — art that demands sustained attention, rewards patience, punishes scanning. Translate: the piece should appear nearly static for the first 30 seconds, then reveal a slow transformation that becomes apparent over 60-120s of continuous viewing (color drift across regions, particles migrating in and out of dense zones, a hidden form emerging through fog). No sudden events. No clear loops. The viewer who scrolls past sees nothing; the one who waits sees the work. Display a tiny breath-counter in the corner so the patient viewer is acknowledged.

Channel POST-HUMAN / MORE-THAN-HUMAN aesthetics (the 2020s expansion of relational aesthetics — Donna Haraway's 'kin', Anna Tsing's 'mushroom at the end of the world'). Translate: the piece's behaviour should look NOT-HUMAN-CENTERED. Slime mold pheromone trails, fungal anastomosis, ant decision-making, microbial mat layering — pick one non-human cognition and let it drive the visual. Avoid the human gaze: no portrait orientation, no symmetric composition, no center-stage. The piece should feel like watching a forest floor at night, with nothing performing for you.

Channel biological-system aesthetics — emergence, local feedback, growth that looks alive (not animated, alive). Pick one: {system}. The piece should respond to local conditions, exhibit feedback loops, develop over time, have a tendency. Avoid mechanical periodicity; embrace organic timescales (slow growth, occasional bursts, healing, decay). Form should EMERGE rather than be drawn. No two viewing sessions should look identical — randomness in the rules, determinism in the dynamics.
params: Turing reaction-diffusion (Gray-Scott U+V system, spots/stripes/spirals depending on F+k parameters)

coral polyp colony (DLA biased by a sunlight gradient — particles aggregate preferentially toward light)
cellular slime mold aggregation (single cells that cluster on starvation, form pseudoplasmodium, migrate)
ant pheromone trail formation (agents drop pheromone, sense ahead, bias toward strongest — Sage Jenson's physarum is one specialization)
Lichtenberg figure / dielectric breakdown (DLA with electrical-field bias — branching lightning-tree)
embryonic gastrulation (sheet of cells folding inward to form layers — topological transformation)
